title: Freya and the Winter
premise: Lena Brightwater hosts a small-town overnight radio show, but lately the callers are people the town buried last week—and they all ask about 'the extra chair' in her grandmother's photographs. Digging into her inheritance of the old Brightwater house, Lena learns the town's founders bound a hungry winter presence beneath it, and every generation a family must keep the ritual alive by remaining unseen and uncounted. When the presence marks Lena by name on air, invisibility fails, and she must complete the founders' interrupted rite—offering not a life, but the truth the town has lied about for a century. In the end, Lena broadcasts the whole confession live, letting the town finally witness what it buried; the winter releases its hold, the extra chair empties, and Lena signs off at dawn, no longer invisible but free.
about_author: Zephyrine Galloway is the pen name of a former late-night radio producer who spent years answering calls from strangers who sounded like they were calling from very far away. They write horror about small towns that keep their secrets warm.

chapters.title: The Dead Air Hour
chapters.summary: POV Lena. On her 2 a.m. call-in show, a listener describes his own funeral from last Tuesday. Lena assumes a prank until he mentions her grandmother's name. Emotional beat: unease disguised as professional calm; Lena keeps talking because silence feels more dangerous than the impossible voice.

chapters.title: Inventory of Doors
chapters.summary: POV Lena. Lena moves into the inherited Brightwater house and catalogs its oddities: eleven doors, ten rooms, lights that must stay on. A neighbor warns her to never count aloud after dark. Emotional beat: loneliness curdling into watchfulness as the house begins to feel occupied.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: POV Lena. Sorting grandma's photo albums, Lena notices every picture—from 1948 to last spring—includes one more chair than there should be, always empty, always angled toward the camera. Emotional beat: dread arriving quietly through domestic detail; the past was never still.

chapters.title: Callers
chapters.summary: POV Lena. More dead listeners phone in, each asking whether she has 'finished counting.' The station manager hears nothing on the logs—dead air where Lena hears voices. Emotional beat: isolation deepening; only Lena can hear the audience that shouldn't exist.

chapters.title: What the Founders Buried
chapters.summary: POV Lena, with archive interludes. At the historical society, Lena finds the founders' ledger: a pact binding 'the Winter' beneath the Brightwater land, renewed each generation by a family sworn to stay unseen. Emotional beat: inheritance reframed as obligation, not gift.

chapters.title: The Neighbor Who Wasn't There
chapters.summary: POV Lena. Her helpful neighbor Mrs. Voss appears in a 1961 photograph—unchanged. Confronted, Voss admits she is part of the ritual's old guard, kept alive to keep watch. Emotional beat: betrayal braided with relief; Lena isn't alone, but allies come with debts.

chapters.title: Counting to Eleven
chapters.summary: POV Lena. After midnight, Lena counts the doors aloud: eleven. The house rearranges itself around the number, and something answers from behind the eleventh door, patient and cold. Emotional beat: first direct contact with the Winter; curiosity punished.

chapters.title: Signal Bleed
chapters.summary: POV Dev, station engineer. Dev discovers the dead callers' audio matches recordings of a 1974 broadcast that was never aired—a confession cut off mid-sentence. Emotional beat: rational man confronting evidence he can't shred; loyalty to Lena vs. self-preservation.

chapters.title: The Unseen Clause
chapters.summary: POV Lena. Voss explains the rule: the Brightwaters survive by being overlooked—no photos facing them, no names spoken, no counting. Grandma broke protocol by keeping albums. The chair appeared the day Lena inherited. Emotional beat: grief for a grandmother whose love endangered her.

chapters.title: Frost on the Inside
chapters.summary: POV Lena. Frost blooms on interior windows; breath hangs indoors; the radio plays static shaped like breathing. Townspeople begin greeting Lena without seeing her—eyes sliding past. Emotional beat: the horror of becoming invisible exactly when visibility means survival.

chapters.title: The Interrupted Broadcast
chapters.summary: POV Dev. Dev restores the 1974 tape: Lena's grandmother, mid-ritual, confessing the founders' crime—they didn't bind the Winter, they made it, feeding it a sacrificed child to buy the town prosperity. The tape ends with a scream and a promise: 'the last Brightwater will finish it.' Emotional beat: revelation as wound.

chapters.title: What the Town Owes
chapters.summary: POV Lena. Lena confronts the town council, descendants of the founders, who admit everything and beg her to simply disappear like her grandmother did. Emotional beat: fury at complicity dressed as tradition; loyalty to the town vs. truth.

chapters.title: The Chair Sits Down
chapters.summary: POV Lena. The extra chair is no longer empty in new photographs—something sits in it now, wearing the shape of the sacrificed child. It speaks through the radio during dead air: 'You promised.' Emotional beat: terror tempered by terrible empathy for the victim at the story's center.

chapters.title: Dev's Decision
chapters.summary: POV Dev. Ordered by the council to erase the tapes, Dev instead copies them and schedules an unsanctioned broadcast. He knows it may cost him everything. Emotional beat: quiet heroism; choosing truth over safety.

chapters.title: Ritual of Small Hours
chapters.summary: POV Lena. Following the ledger, Lena attempts the rite alone at 3:33 a.m.: naming the child, returning what was taken. She falters—the rite requires witnesses, a town that sees. The Winter takes her voice for a night. Emotional beat: failure and humility; rituals need community, not sacrifice.

chapters.title: Whiteout
chapters.summary: POV Lena. The Winter escalates: snow falls indoors, the town goes silent, phones ring with the voices of everyone who ever died owing the Brightwaters anything. Voss burns as a warning. Emotional beat: siege horror; time visibly running out as frost reaches Lena's chest.

chapters.title: The Confession Draft
chapters.summary: POV Lena. Writing her own broadcast script, Lena decides the rite's true form: the founders' lie must be spoken publicly, witnessed, mourned. She visits the unmarked grave of the sacrificed child, Edda, and apologizes. Emotional beat: resolve born of grief; truth as offering.

chapters.title: Going Live
chapters.summary: POV alternating Lena/Dev. Against the council's threats, Dev opens the transmitter; Lena reads the founders' crime, the ledger, the names, live on air. Across town, listeners stop what they're doing and listen—including the dead. Emotional beat: climax of courage; broadcasting as séance.

chapters.title: Edda
chapters.summary: POV Lena. As the town truly hears, the studio fills with cold and light. Edda appears—not monstrous, just a child waiting a century to be counted. Lena says her name, and the town, listening, says it too. Emotional beat: catharsis; witnessing as the completion of the ritual.

chapters.title: Thaw
chapters.summary: POV Lena. The Winter recedes door by door; the eleventh door opens onto an ordinary wall. The dead callers sign off one by one, grateful. The chair vanishes from every photograph, including the oldest ones—as if it had never been needed. Emotional beat: release; mourning finally allowed to end.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: POV Lena. Weeks later, Lena keeps the show, now taking calls from the living. The house has ten doors again; she leaves the lights on out of habit, not fear. The council resigns; the ledger goes to the museum. Emotional beat: bittersweet peace; belonging earned through truth.

chapters.title: Last Call
chapters.summary: POV Lena, final scene. On the anniversary, one last caller rings in—a child's voice saying only 'thank you,' then dial tone. Lena smiles, says goodnight to the town, and lets the static run a moment before cutting the feed. Emotional beat: closure with a shiver; some frequencies are never fully empty.
